# What Makes a Case Study Believable

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-makes-a-case-study-believable/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-21 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A case study is evidence, not advertising. A believable one keeps the specific situation, the real sequence including setbacks, dated numbers with a baseline and the customer's own voice, even when the name has to go. Research on reviews and two-sided messages suggests some acknowledged weakness raises credibility, and US rules treat testimonials as claims that need substantiation.

A prospective customer reads your case study to learn one thing: have you solved a problem like mine, and can you show me what happened? A logo, a polished testimonial and a large percentage will not answer that on their own. A believable case study reads like an account of a project: the starting situation, the decisions made, what changed with a baseline and a date, and what the evidence cannot support. Research on reviews suggests a little visible imperfection raises trust, and in the US, the FTC treats claims made through testimonials as claims the advertiser must substantiate.

## Start with a situation the reader recognises

"We helped a fintech company grow" tells a potential client almost nothing. What kind of fintech company? Was it struggling to acquire users, get partners to respond or explain a complex product? What could the team afford to try? Which constraints made the job difficult?

For example, an anonymous payments start-up with a two-person sales team and a limited marketing budget is already more useful context than "a leading fintech innovator." The reader can judge whether the example resembles their own business.

Then explain what the provider actually did. Do not say it "optimised the growth engine." Say that it rewrote an unclear landing page, interviewed five customers, launched a partner referral campaign or stopped spending on ads that brought the wrong people. The specific work is the useful part of the story.

| Element | Weak version | Believable version |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Situation | "A leading fintech innovator" | An anonymous payments start-up, two sellers, limited budget, partners not responding |
| Work | "Optimised the growth engine" | Rewrote the landing page, interviewed five customers, launched partner referrals |
| Result | "Leads up 40%" | Qualified demo requests from 10 to 14 a month over eight weeks |
| Limits | None stated | The sales process changed too, so the result cannot be attributed to one activity |
| Cost | Omitted | The time, people and budget the work required |
| Voice | "They were amazing to work with" | The customer describing what was hard or surprising |

## A percentage needs a starting point and a date

Imagine a case study that says "qualified leads increased 40%." Did the company go from five to seven leads a month, or 500 to 700? Was this measured over a week or a year? Did the sales team also hire more people or change the definition of a qualified lead?

**Hard to evaluate:** "We boosted qualified leads by 40% through our proprietary approach."

**Much more useful:** "In this illustrative eight-week project, monthly qualified demo requests rose from 10 to 14 after changes to the website and partner outreach. The team also changed its sales process, so the result cannot be attributed to one activity alone."

Both statements are illustrative, not real campaign results. The second tells a reader what the number means and what remains uncertain. That is more valuable than an enormous percentage with no baseline.

Be just as clear about the cost of the work. If the result required six months of engineering, a new salesperson and a large advertising budget, that matters to a buyer deciding whether the approach is realistic for them.

## Why setbacks make the story more credible

Real projects involve delays, wrong assumptions and changes in direction. Perhaps the first set of ads attracted too many irrelevant visitors. Maybe the original message confused customers. Or a potential partner declined to participate, forcing a different approach.

The research on persuasion supports including them. Martin Eisend's 2006 meta-analysis of two-sided advertising, messages that admit a weakness alongside strengths, found the effect depends on how much negative information is included, and that the relationship with brand attitude is curvilinear: some acknowledged weakness helps, too much hurts. Consumer review data point the same way. Northwestern University's Spiegel Research Center, analysing PowerReviews data across more than 40 product categories, found purchase likelihood peaks when average ratings sit between 4.2 and 4.5 stars and falls as they approach a perfect 5. It also cited PowerReviews research that 82% of shoppers seek out negative reviews.

Retail ratings are not B2B case studies, but the mechanism is general. Include one or two meaningful decisions the team changed because of what it learned. That lets the reader see judgment in action rather than a flawless sequence written after the fact.

> A case study with no setbacks reads as edited. One honest correction does more for credibility than five adjectives.

## Testimonials are claims, too

A direct customer comment can help, especially when it describes what was difficult or surprising. But a quote is not proof of every claimed outcome.

The US Federal Trade Commission's revised Guides Concerning the Use of Endorsements and Testimonials in Advertising, effective 26 July 2023, are specific. Advertisers must have adequate substantiation for claims made through endorsements, just as for claims they make directly; "consumer endorsements themselves are not competent and reliable scientific evidence." And when a testimonial describes a result on a key attribute, the ad is likely to be read as saying that result is typical. If the advertiser cannot substantiate that, it must clearly disclose what people can generally expect.

The FTC went further in August 2024 with a final rule on consumer reviews and testimonials, effective 21 October 2024. It prohibits creating or disseminating testimonials that misrepresent whether the person exists, whether they used the product or service, or what their experience was. Morgan Lewis's summary notes penalties of up to $51,744 per violation, adjusted annually for inflation.

The practical rule: a happy customer can describe their experience; factual performance claims still need evidence you can produce.

## When the client cannot be named

For regulated financial products, enterprise infrastructure and competitive projects, naming the client or sharing exact figures may not be allowed. That does not mean the case study must become useless. It does mean the provider needs explicit permission for whatever it publishes.

Describe the business problem, type of customer, work and outcome at a level the client approves. Use ranges or percentages only when the underlying figures are real and the client agrees to that presentation. Be careful: revealing the geography, company size, product category and timeline together may identify a customer even without its name.

Ask for approval of the project description, individual quotes, performance claims and any screenshots. A composite story based on several engagements may be useful as an industry observation, but it must be labelled as a composite and never passed off as a single verified customer result.

## When you do not have a case study yet

Do not manufacture one. Instead, show how you would approach a problem: the questions you would ask, what you would inspect, the work you would try first, and what evidence you would need before recommending more spending.

Then make case-study permission part of the next engagement. Agree early which measurements can be retained and whether the customer might approve a public or anonymous summary. You cannot force an endorsement, but you can make it easier to document real work without scrambling for data months later. A [win-loss analysis](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-win-loss-analysis/) of recent deals will show which proof buyers actually asked for, and our piece on [proposal standards](https://lowob.com/research/proposal-standards/) covers where that proof belongs in a bid.

One believable story about a modest result is more useful than five vaguely impressive success stories. In the terms of [content with a job](https://lowob.com/research/content-with-a-job/), a case study serves the supplier-selection stage, and its reader is usually the evaluator who has to defend the choice to everyone else.

## lowob takeaways

- **Show the starting situation.** The buyer needs to recognise the problem, the customer and the constraints.
- **Make results checkable.** Baseline, time period, method and what else changed.
- **Keep the setbacks.** Some acknowledged weakness raises credibility; a flawless story does not.
- **Treat testimonials as claims.** Substantiate what they imply, get approval, and label composites.

## Next move

Before publishing your next customer story, give it to someone outside the project and ask them to name the baseline, the time period, the cost and one thing that went wrong. Anything they cannot find, add or cut.
